Just now

--

By Aditya
I’ve probably had a version of the same conversation with five different people this week. Someone sends me a clip from Jantar Mantar, a van with cameras on it, screens flashing names and photos, and asks some version of “wait, is this actually reading faces in real time?” And every time, I end up typing out a mini explanation in the DMs. So I figured I’d just write the whole thing properly once.

For anyone who missed it: student protests have been going on at Jantar Mantar, and videos started circulating of a Delhi Police vehicle called Ikshana, apparently running facial recognition on the crowd. A few reports (Tribune, The Print, MediaNama) filled in more detail. Two vehicles were parked near the site. One was streaming CCTV footage back to officers, and the other was running facial recognition software against a police database, reportedly to catch people with existing criminal records rather than to log every single protester. People online also started asking if this was connected to Aadhaar. As of now, nobody has confirmed that. It’s floating around as a theory, not a fact, and the difference matters.
That’s really all I want to say about the protest itself. What I actually care about, and what I think most people got wrong or oversimplified in their takes, is how this technology works underneath. “Facial recognition” gets used like it’s one magic button someone presses, and as someone who spends a lot of time in security and ML adjacent stuff, that flattening bugs me a little. So let’s actually open it up.
Your face doesn’t get stored. A version of it, made of numbers, does.
This was the part that genuinely reshaped how I thought about the whole thing when I first read into it properly. A facial recognition system isn’t sitting there comparing your photo to another photo like a human would. It converts your face into a list of numbers, and compares number lists.
There’s a full pipeline behind that one sentence, and it’s worth walking through slowly.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

First, the system has to actually spot a face in the frame. A raw camera feed is just pixels to a computer, no different structurally than a photo of a wall. So step one is scanning each frame for anything shaped like a human face and drawing a box around it, regardless of who’s in it. This is handled by detection models like RetinaFace or MTCNN, and they’re fast enough now to do this live, across a moving crowd, in bad lighting, at weird angles. Those green boxes people noticed around faces in the viral clips, that’s this step running in real time.
Once a face is found, it needs to be straightened out. Nobody stands perfectly facing a camera in real life. The system locates landmark points, corners of the eyes, tip of the nose, edge of the jaw, and uses those to mentally rotate the face into a standard front-facing position before doing anything else with it. Skip this and every step after it gets noisier.
Then comes the part I actually find impressive. A neural network, trained on millions of faces beforehand, takes that aligned image and compresses it into a vector, usually somewhere around 128 to 512 numbers. This is called an embedding. It’s encoding things like the distance between your eyes, your cheekbone geometry, your jawline, all as numbers a machine can do arithmetic on. You can’t easily reverse this back into a photo. It’s not a mugshot sitting in a folder somewhere. Think of it more like GPS coordinates that place your face at one exact point in a massive, imaginary map of every possible face.
All of these coordinates live in something called a vector database. Every face a system already “knows,” say from a database of past offenders, gets stored as one of these points. When a new face comes in off a live camera, the system isn’t flipping through stored faces one at a time like a photo album. It runs a nearest-neighbour search (FAISS and HNSW are the usual tools for this) and instantly finds whichever stored points sit closest to the new one.
Closeness gets turned into a score, something like 91% or 84%, and this is genuinely where most of the real-world risk in these systems lives. Not in the neural network itself, but in one human decision made way before deployment: where to set the confidence threshold, the cutoff below which a match doesn’t count. Push that threshold too low and you get false positives, innocent people getting flagged. Push it too high and you get false negatives, real matches slipping through unnoticed. There’s no objectively correct number here. Someone picks it, and that choice quietly shapes everything downstream, usually without any public visibility into what number they landed on.
Some systems add a liveness check on top, confirming the face in front of the camera belongs to an actual person physically present, not a printed photo or a video replay. This matters a lot for something like unlocking your phone. It matters far less for a van scanning a crowd from thirty feet away, which is part of why liveness isn’t really the interesting question in the Jantar Mantar case.
And then, in theory, there’s supposed to be a human checking the machine’s output before anyone acts on it. A match from the algorithm is meant to be treated as a lead for an operator to review, not an automatic verdict. This is the step I think about the most, honestly, because it’s also the one we almost never get to see. Whether that review is genuinely careful, or just someone glancing at a screen and nodding along, happens entirely inside a control room. We don’t get a window into that part.
None of this runs without a lot of unglamorous hardware
It’s easy to talk about AI as some abstract cloud thing, but a live facial recognition system needs real infrastructure sitting underneath it, and I think that infrastructure tells you a lot about what’s actually possible versus what sounds impressive in a headline.
Camera placement and resolution matter more than most people assume. A face that’s too small in the frame, too blurry, or angled too far away from the lens might never produce a usable embedding, no matter how good the model behind it is.
A lot of the initial processing now happens at the edge, meaning right at the camera or inside a vehicle like Ikshana, rather than sending raw video all the way to a distant server first. This cuts down on lag and network load, which matters when you’re handling dozens of camera feeds simultaneously.
GPUs are what make the model side fast enough to actually be useful. Detection and feature extraction are computationally expensive tasks, and without dedicated hardware acceleration you’d be waiting minutes per frame rather than getting near-instant matches.
Then there’s the database itself, the list of known faces being matched against, whether that’s prior offenders or missing persons, sitting on centralized servers that all these edge devices are constantly talking to over a network that has to stay fast and stable.

Places you’re probably already using this without thinking twice
I think most people picture facial recognition purely as a surveillance tool, but honestly it’s woven into daily life in ways most of us are completely fine with, which I find kind of telling.
Face ID on your phone runs basically the same detection and embedding pipeline I just described, except it happens entirely on your device, which is a big reason it feels private even though it’s technically the “same” tech people get nervous about elsewhere. Airports use it at e-gates to match travelers against their passport photos. Some banks use it during KYC when you open an account. Schools and offices use it for attendance instead of swipe cards. A few retailers have tried it for loss prevention, though that use case has gotten a lot of pushback in several countries. And there are genuinely well-documented cases of it helping identify missing children and trafficking victims, which to me is one of the more compelling reasons this technology exists at all.
The bigger picture in India, and how other countries compare
Delhi Police isn’t the only one using this. Facial recognition has been spreading across Indian policing quietly for a few years now.
Punjab Police has something called PAIS (Punjab Artificial Intelligence System), tied into their CCTV network to help identify suspects and track vehicles. At the national level, the NCRB has been building the Automated Facial Recognition System (AFRS), a proposed shared database meant to let police across different states search criminal records using facial images. It’s been delayed repeatedly, and it’s drawn a fair bit of criticism from privacy researchers, mostly because it’s being built without any dedicated law governing how facial data can be collected or used.
And that’s really the core gap for India right now. There’s no law written specifically for facial recognition. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 covers personal data generally, but law enforcement’s use of biometric surveillance sits in a much murkier zone, leaning on constitutional principles and case-by-case court rulings rather than a clear rulebook. Which is exactly what the Delhi High Court petition is trying to push on right now.
Zoom out globally and the picture gets genuinely varied. The US has no single federal law on this. A few cities banned police use of it outright at one point, while federal agencies use it under their own internal policies, and there have been real, documented wrongful arrests tied to bad matches. The UK’s Metropolitan Police has run some of the most closely studied live facial recognition trials anywhere, and they’ve taken heavy scrutiny over both accuracy and legal grounding. China runs what’s probably the most extensive facial recognition network on the planet, built into everyday transit and public life at a scale nowhere else really matches. Singapore uses it in a tightly controlled way through its national digital ID system, SingPass. Dubai has poured serious money into “smart city” surveillance as part of a broader AI-driven governance strategy. And the EU has taken arguably the strictest stance among major economies, with the AI Act explicitly labeling real-time biometric identification in public spaces as high-risk and restricting it to narrow situations, like searching for a missing person or stopping an imminent terror threat.
Put India next to all of that and we land somewhere in the middle. Real, active use by law enforcement, but without the kind of dedicated legal framework that either restricts it clearly, like the EU, or at least attempts to define it, like even the more permissive countries have tried.
Why this makes people uneasy, and why the police side isn’t nothing either
I want to be fair to both sides here, because I think this topic gets flattened way too often into “surveillance bad” versus “safety good,” and neither framing is honest by itself.
The concerns from researchers and privacy advocates are real. Most people captured in public deployments are never asked for consent, and often don’t know it’s happening at all, which raises a genuinely fair question about whether being in a public space should automatically mean your face is fair game for biometric logging. There’s also a real chilling effect worth taking seriously. Even if nothing bad ever happens to a specific person, just knowing you might be scanned at a protest changes whether some people choose to show up, and that has real implications for something as basic as the right to assemble. Bias is another one I take seriously, not as a talking point but because the research backs it up. Independent studies from places like MIT Media Lab and NIST have repeatedly found that many facial recognition systems have noticeably higher error rates for women and for people with darker skin
